title: How Burnham should engage with Africa
gist: As UK bilateral aid to Africa faces a 52% cut over three years to fund higher defence spending, Chatham House argues Burnham's government should compensate with sharper commercial strategy, greater use of export-finance and development-finance instruments, and institutional reforms that treat Africa as a strategic partner rather than a development-aid recipient.

themes.theme: UK's Africa policy framework under Burnham

insights.claim: The UK's Approach to Africa, developed in 2025 under then-Foreign Secretary David Lammy after consultations with African partners, sets out a pragmatic vision centred on trade and investment links, but it remains a framework for engagement rather than a full strategic reset of UK-Africa relations.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Investors should not expect a wholesale policy overhaul from London; commercial opportunities will emerge incrementally through existing programmes rather than a new grand strategy.
insights.locator: The UK's Approach to Africa, developed in 2025

insights.claim: Africa is unlikely to be among new UK prime minister Andy Burnham's first foreign policy priorities, even though the continent's expanding consumer markets, long-term growth potential and central role in future supply chains have made it an arena of intensifying global competition.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Political attention (and therefore diplomatic and financial resourcing) toward Africa may lag its rising economic relevance, a gap other powers could exploit.
insights.locator: Africa is unlikely to be among new prime minister

insights.claim: Burnham's government needs to define a clear ambition for UK engagement with Africa and translate it into a credible, differentiated offer that advances both African priorities and UK interests, given a challenging fiscal environment that is reducing bilateral funding for African countries to help finance higher defence spending.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The credibility of UK commercial and diplomatic offers to Africa will depend on execution, not just stated ambition, over the next parliamentary term.
insights.locator: Burnham also faces a challenging fiscal environment

insights.claim: The UK government's latest spending plans amount to a 52 per cent reduction in regional bilateral aid to Africa over the next three years, as part of wider cuts to fund higher defence spending, which will drastically impact long-term programming and could damage perceptions of the UK's commitment to the continent.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A 52% aid cut is a material signal for organizations and investors tracking UK development-finance flows into Africa; programme continuity and grant-funded initiatives are at elevated risk over the next three years.
insights.quote: a 52 per cent reduction in regional bilateral aid to Africa over the next three years as part of wider cuts to fund higher defence spending
insights.locator: The UK government's latest spending plans amount to

insights.claim: Despite the aid cuts, the UK has maintained strategic partnerships with regional heavyweights including Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa, remains active on Sudan through humanitarian assistance and diplomacy, and continues security and stabilization engagement in conflict-affected regions through instruments such as the Integrated Security Fund.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: These three markets remain the most likely near-term focal points for continued UK diplomatic and commercial bandwidth despite overall budget cuts.
insights.locator: Yet they do not represent a total disengagement

insights.claim: Selective UK support for conflict prevention and resolution, including mediation efforts in Sudan, needs to remain part of the UK's approach alongside sustained humanitarian engagement even as other programmes face cuts.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Sudan-focused humanitarian and mediation channels are likely to be protected budget lines even as broader bilateral aid contracts.
insights.locator: Selective support for conflict prevention and resolution

themes.theme: Trade and investment coherence: lessons from Germany

insights.claim: Germany's 'Marshall Plan with Africa' links development finance, industrial policy and private sector mobilization through various reform partnerships with select African countries, combining policy reforms with targeted finance to improve the investment climate and attract private capital.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Germany's coordinated reform-plus-finance model is a template for how bilateral programmes can crowd in private capital; UK-linked vehicles adopting similar discipline could unlock parallel opportunities.

insights.claim: Rather than replicating Germany's model outright, the UK can adopt its underlying discipline of setting sharper priorities, strengthening cross-government coordination and presenting a single business-oriented offer focused on areas where UK and African countries' interests align.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A more joined-up UK government offer (spanning trade, development finance and industrial policy) would be a signal that commercial engagement with Africa is becoming better coordinated and easier to navigate for investors.

themes.theme: Critical minerals as an alignment-of-interest opportunity

insights.claim: Resource-rich countries including the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Zambia and Namibia are seeking to move beyond raw resource extraction toward greater industrial development and value creation, and the UK Critical Minerals Strategy aims to build more resilient mineral supply chains for the energy transition and emerging technologies.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Downstream processing and value-addition projects in DRC, Zambia and Namibia are the emerging opportunity set, not just raw ore extraction — investors should track industrial partnerships, not just mining licenses.
insights.locator: Critical minerals offer a clear example

insights.claim: The alignment of UK and African interests in critical minerals presents an opportunity not simply to secure resource access for the UK, but to build partnerships supporting investment, skills development, infrastructure and local economic transformation.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Deals framed around local value-creation (skills, infrastructure) rather than pure extraction may face less political resistance and attract more African government support.
insights.locator: This alignment of interests presents an opportunity

insights.claim: The Lobito Corridor illustrates how digitization is becoming a factor shaping competition over critical minerals in Africa.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Digital infrastructure and data systems are becoming an underappreciated competitive lever in mineral-corridor geopolitics, worth monitoring alongside physical logistics investment.

themes.theme: Public finance instruments to mobilize private capital

insights.claim: UK Export Finance (the UK's export credit agency) and British International Investment (its development finance institution) can help de-risk projects, boost co-financing and support commercially viable investments in Africa that might otherwise stall.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: These two institutions are the practical entry points for private investors seeking blended-finance or guarantee-backed exposure to African infrastructure and energy deals.
insights.locator: The UK can also make more strategic use

insights.claim: The Simandou 2040 programme in Guinea demonstrates this approach in practice: a UK Export Finance guarantee of £1.8 billion is supporting a portfolio of infrastructure projects aligned with the Simandou iron ore development, helping catalyse wider international investment in transport, energy and administrative modernization.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A concrete £1.8bn UKEF guarantee tied to Simandou iron ore is a live, sizeable case study of UK-backed infrastructure finance in Africa that investors in the mining and logistics supply chain should track.
insights.quote: a UK Export Finance guarantee of £1.8 billion is supporting a portfolio of infrastructure projects aligned with the Simandou iron ore development
insights.locator: The Simandou 2040 programme in Guinea demonstrates

insights.claim: Harnessing the depth of the City of London's financial markets and asset managers will be essential to turning UK-backed investment pipelines into large-scale capital flows for African infrastructure, energy and industrial projects.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: London-based asset managers and capital markets are positioned as the scaling mechanism for African infrastructure finance beyond what government guarantees alone can provide.
insights.locator: At the same time, harnessing the depth

insights.claim: A ministerial structure that separates Africa from development responsibilities, supported by a dedicated Africa adviser to the prime minister, would strengthen cross-government coordination and signal that the UK views African countries as strategic partners rather than primarily as aid recipients.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A watchable near-term policy marker: whether Burnham creates a distinct Africa portfolio separate from development would indicate whether the strategic-partner rhetoric is being institutionalized.
insights.locator: A ministerial structure that separates Africa

insights.claim: Further reductions to UK diplomatic missions in Africa should be avoided, as recent budget pressures and organizational changes have already constrained the UK's presence and further cuts would weaken in-country expertise, trade and investment capacity, and trusted networks underpinning commercial engagement.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Shrinking embassy footprints is a leading indicator of reduced UK commercial intelligence and deal-sourcing capacity on the continent, a risk factor for UK-linked investors relying on diplomatic networks.
insights.locator: Recent budget pressures and organizational changes

insights.claim: The UK's upcoming G20 presidency in 2027 provides a timely opportunity for the UK to support African ambitions for global governance reform, greater representation in multilateral institutions and a stronger African voice in forums such as the G20.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The 2027 UK G20 presidency is a concrete, dated catalyst to watch for African-representation initiatives and any related diplomatic or commercial announcements.
insights.locator: The UK's upcoming G20 presidency in 2027

insights.claim: Technical cooperation on public financial management, taxation, digital governance and project preparation often delivers greater long-term value to African partners than headline funding alone, because it responds directly to their priorities and strengthens foundations for sustainable growth.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Lower-cost technical-assistance programmes may prove more durable and relationship-building for the UK than large capital transfers, especially under tightened aid budgets.

insights.claim: Soft power in UK-Africa relations remains important but is increasingly exercised through practical cooperation, such as education, professional exchanges, research partnerships and institutional cooperation, rather than traditional influence-building.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Education and research-partnership programmes are a lower-profile but potentially higher-ROI channel for sustaining UK-Africa ties amid shrinking aid budgets.
